description: I am a student interested in space, technology, design, and creative problem-solving. My interests include UI/UX, web development, graphic design, data visualization, and storytelling. For the CLPS Lunar Mission Browser challenge, I aim to create an engaging way to explore lunar mission information. I am looking for teammates interested in software, science, data, AI/ML, visualization, and related areas.
summary: Echoes Beyond Earth is a website for children aged 8 to 12 where machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars tell their own stories in the first person. Visitors pick a machine from a simplified Moon map or a list and read what it was, why it was sent, and what it discovered, with quick facts and a link to the NASA page behind each story. The first version covers Apollo 11’s Eagle landing stage, Apollo 15’s Falcon and its science station, and Mars Pathfinder’s Sojourner rover. It answers the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge by turning NASA’s records into short, accurate stories that connect the engineering of each machine to the science it made possible.
details: The site is a single web page built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and SVG drawings, hosted on GitHub Pages. A welcome page explains how to explore. Visitors choose a machine from a simplified Moon map (a latitude and longitude grid with markers placed from NASA’s landing coordinates; it is not a precise map) or from a list. Each machine tells its story in the first person, with a drawing, quick facts, a “Where am I now?” box and a link to its NASA page. The stories are paraphrased from three NASA pages and are written for ages 8 to 12. The aim is to make children feel a personal connection to the machines and curious about the science they did. We used no photos or outside media: all drawings are made in code. An AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) helped write the code, the text and the drawings, and this is acknowledged on the website and in the slides. Future versions could add more machines from NASA’s list and a Mars map.
